issues.legal_issue: Government tax arrears take priority over an unsecured private debt owed by the same debtor.
material_facts: A private creditor obtained a decree against a debtor and attached part of a security deposit held for the debtor.
The government claimed income-tax arrears from the same debtor and sought the attached money toward those arrears.
issues.conclusion: The government was entitled to priority over the private creditor in recovering the tax arrears from the attached money.
issues.legal_principle: The common-law doctrine of priority applies to tax debts owed to the government over unsecured debts owed to private creditors. The Court relied on the weight of Indian authority, including The Secretary of State in Council for India v. The Bombay Landing & Shipping Co., Manickam Chettiar v. Income-tax Officer, Bank of India v. John Bowman, and Bell v. The Municipal Commissioners for the City of Madras. It disapproved the contrary observations in Ramachandra v. Pitchaikanni and disapproved Kaka Mohammad Ghouse Sahib & Co. v. United Commercial Syndicate. The justification for priority is that the State needs tax revenue to perform its governmental functions.

rule.if: tax_priority_dispute_case and government_tax_arrears_due and same_debtor_claims_compete and private_claim_is_unsecured

predicates.tax_priority_dispute_case: A dispute concerns the priority of a government claim for tax arrears over a private creditor's claim to a debtor's assets.
predicates.government_tax_arrears_due: The debtor owes tax arrears to the government.
predicates.same_debtor_claims_compete: The government and a private creditor seek recovery from assets of the same debtor.
predicates.private_claim_is_unsecured: The private creditor's claim is not secured by the debtor's property.

issues.definition: When tax arrears owed by a debtor compete with an unsecured private claim against that debtor, the government tax claim takes priority.

issues.legal_issue: A common-law rule concerning substantive rights that was adopted and applied before the Constitution remains law in force after the Constitution takes effect.
material_facts: The priority rule was based on common law and had been applied and upheld by courts in the relevant territory before the Constitution took effect.
The dispute concerned the continued operation of that rule after the Constitution took effect.
issues.conclusion: The common-law priority rule, having been adopted and judicially applied in the relevant territory before the Constitution, continued as law in force after the Constitution took effect.
issues.legal_principle: Article 372(1) continues laws in force immediately before the Constitution until they are altered, repealed, or amended by a competent authority. In Director of Rationing and Distribution v. The Corporation of Calcutta, the Court held that “laws in force” include common law adopted and applied in India. The Court applied that reasoning to substantive common-law rules recognized by Indian judicial decisions.

predicates.constitutional_continuity_case: A case concerns whether a rule applied before the Constitution continues to operate after it takes effect.
predicates.substantive_common_law_rule: The rule concerns a substantive right rather than merely a method of construing legislation.
predicates.rule_adopted_and_applied_before_constitu: Courts in the relevant territory adopted and applied the rule before the Constitution took effect.

issues.definition: If a substantive common-law rule was adopted and applied in the relevant territory before the Constitution, it continues to operate after the Constitution takes effect.

issues.legal_issue: Legislation that prescribes procedures for recovering tax arrears and public demands does not displace the common-law priority rule unless it provides for that priority.
material_facts: The tax legislation provided for recovery of arrears as if they were arrears of land revenue and included other recovery methods.
The public-demands legislation prescribed procedures for recovering public demands, including a procedure for property held by a court or public officer.
Neither statutory scheme provided for the priority of tax arrears over private debts.
issues.conclusion: The tax-recovery provisions and the public-demands recovery legislation did not displace the government’s common-law priority for tax arrears.
issues.legal_principle: Section 46 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, prescribed methods for recovering tax arrears but did not address priority between tax debts and private debts. The Public Demands Recovery Act and its Rule 22 primarily prescribed recovery procedure; Rule 22 could be used because tax arrears were recoverable as public demands, not because it determined priority. The Court distinguished Governor-General in Council v. Shiromani Sugar Mills Ltd., which concerned an express statutory scheme for preferential payments in liquidation, and considered Attorney-General v. De Keyser’s Royal Hotel, Ltd. on the effect of legislation occupying a field previously governed by prerogative.

predicates.statutory_displacement_case: A case concerns whether legislation governing the recovery of tax or public demands displaces a pre-existing priority rule.
predicates.tax_recovery_law_prescribes_collection_m: The tax-recovery law sets out methods for collecting tax arrears without determining their priority over private debts.
predicates.public_demand_law_prescribes_recovery_pr: The law governing public demands provides procedures for their recovery.
predicates.legislation_does_not_provide_for_competi: The relevant legislation does not specify the priority between government tax claims and competing private debts.

issues.definition: When recovery legislation prescribes collection methods or procedures but does not determine priority between competing claims, it does not displace the common-law tax priority.
